text: Housing includes existing household assets and completed housing projects; building housing does not automatically add residents.
Farmland is maintained by local workers. Water, tools, and food rations all affect its ongoing supply.
The tool workshop and recycling jobs remain in Lakeside; expansion, labor, and materials are accounted for locally.
The smelter turns locally recycled material into iron. Production is affected by shortages of raw materials and maintenance.
Clinical care consumes tools and knowledge, and shares provisions with local households.
The old schoolhouse and archives support teaching and knowledge production; teachers still need a steady supply of textbooks.
Water services, medical care, and classrooms continuously consume local materials; public service coverage is based on actual accounting.
Freight yards are locally owned; transfers between cities still depend on actual vehicles, routes, and transport costs.

A local industrial city built on dismantled scrap mines and old smelters. Local basic provisions are self-sufficient, but the smelters run day and night and need a steady supply of maintenance materials.

The three cities share commercial route capacity, while each manages its own household registry and public warehouse. Lakeside supplies grain, Mine Ridge supplies iron, and this city provides tools and specialist services.
